question: If the self is all-at-once consciousness, why does ordinary I-know talk prove nothing?
premises: Even so he never at any time attains separateness in the ultimate sense.
For he is all-at-once, of the nature of consciousness.
Yet the objector voices first-person doing and knowing, asking whether ordinary Mitra-and-Caitra folk do and know likewise.
inference: Simultaneous consciousness-nature is granted, but first-person know-talk is challenged as undistinguishing.
uncertainties: The vocative addressee between teacher and self.
Exact verb-sense of do in the Mitra-Caitra clause.
plain_english: Yet even so he never at any time attains separateness in the ultimate sense — for he is all-at-once, of the nature of consciousness. But surely — O essence of densely packed being-awareness — in awareness, that what I do here is strange, or that I know: would not others too, ordinary Mitras and Caitras, do the same? Or how would they not know?
